javellana:
● Following the facts from Planas (1973), this case determined the constitutionality of the ratification of the 1973 Constitution.
● The question of whether the proposed Constitution had been ratified in accordance with Article XV of the 1935 Constitution was not a political question. It was a matter that the Court could determine by examining the pertinent constitutional and statutory provisions and the acts undertaken to implement them.
● Article XV, Section 1 required ratification in an election or plebiscite held in accordance with law and participated in only by qualified and duly registered voters. Concepcion maintained that the Citizens’ Assemblies established under Presidential Decree No. 86 did not satisfy this requirement. They were composed of citizens aged fifteen and above, rather than being restricted to qualified and duly registered voters. Consequently, participation was not confined to the electorate contemplated by the Constitution and the election laws (Concepcion and Zaldivar).
● The proceedings in the Citizens’ Assemblies involved questions about several matters, including the New Society, reforms under martial law, the convening of Congress, the holding of a later plebiscite, and approval of the proposed Constitution. Concepcion reasoned that these proceedings could not be treated as the plebiscite required for constitutional ratification. The questions were not confined to the ratification issue, and the manner in which the voting was conducted was not within the intendment of Article XV, Section 1, or in accordance with the Election Code of 1971.
● Concepcion held that the reported affirmative votes did not necessarily reflect the people’s genuine acceptance of the proposed Constitution, given his doubts about the freedom of their expression and the accuracy of the voting reports (since it was held during Martial Law). He further maintained that the people’s continued existence under the government did not establish valid ratification or cure noncompliance with Article XV, Section 1 of the 1935 Constitution.

● A people’s initiative to change the Constitution applies only to an amendment of the Constitution and not to its revision.
● The two-part test may be an aid in determining the nature of the change:
1. The quantitative test asks whether the change is “so extensive in its provisions as to directly change the ‘substantial entirety of the Constitution by alteration of existing provisions.”
2. The qualitative test inquires into whether the change will ‘accomplish such far-reaching changes in the nature of our basic governmental plan as to amount to a revision.’
● Under both the quantitative and qualitative tests, the Lambino Group’s initiative is a revision. Quantitatively, the Lambino Group’s changes overhaul Article VI and VII—affecting a total of 105 provisions. Qualitatively, the changes alter substantially the basic governmental plan, from presidential to parliamentary and from a bicameral to a unicameral legislature.
● The Lambino Group’s initiative likewise failed to comply with Article XVII, Section 2 of the Constitution, which requires that an amendment is ‘directly proposed by the people through initiative upon a petition.’ The Section 2 requirement has two elements—first, the people must author and thus, personally sign the proposal. Second, the proposal must be embodied in a petition. The full text of the amendment may be either written on the face of the petition or attached to it. If so attached, the petition must state the fact of such attachment.
● The signature sheet is not the ‘petition’ envisioned in said Section 2. Accordingly, the Lambino Group’s failure to include the text of the amendment in the signature sheet renders the initiative void ________________________________________________________ Dante Gatmaytan, Changing Constitutions: Judicial Review and Redemption in the Philippines (2007)

● General Rule: A suit for acts done in the performance of official functions against an officer of the government which would result in a charge against or financial liability to the government must be regarded as a suit against the State itself although it has not been formally impleaded.

○ The causes of action—injunction and declaration of nullity of award—do not seek to impose a charge against or financial liability to the State but merely to nullify an act by the State.
○ [Obiter dicta] Had PASI additionally sought damages in relation to these causes of action; impleaded the DOTC itself, the suit would have been one against the State itself.

Reading Article XII, Section 11, which prohibits exclusive public utility franchises and permits their amendment when the common good requires, he contended that MORE’s expanded franchise must be justified by the common good, not merely by introducing competition. ● Guidelines of party-list participation:
1. Three different groups may participate in the party-list system → (1) national parties or organizations, (2) regional parties or organizations, and (3) sectoral parties or organizations.
2. National parties or organizations and regional parties or organizations do not need to organize along sectoral lines and do not need to represent any "marginalized & underrepresented" sector.
3. Political parties can participate in party-list elections provided they register under the party-list system and do not field candidates in legislative district elections. a. A political party's sectoral wing is by itself an independent sectoral party, and is linked to a political party through a coalition.
4. Sectoral parties or organizations may either be "marginalized and underrepresented" or lacking in "well-defined political constituencies." It is enough that their principal advocacy pertains to the special interest and concerns of their sector.
5. A majority of the members of sectoral parties or organizations that represent the "marginalized & underrepresented" must belong to the "marginalized & underrepresented" sector they represent. Similarly, a majority of the members of sectoral parties or organizations that lack "well-defined political constituencies" must belong to the sector they represent. a. The nominees of sectoral parties or organizations that represent the "marginalized and underrepresented," or that represent those who lack "well-defined political constituencies," either must belong to their respective sectors, or must have a track record of advocacy for their respective sectors. b. The nominees of national and regional parties or organizations must be bona-fide members of such parties or organizations.

● The Acero Group questioned before the SEC the election of directors of IPI, while Assemblyman Fernandez initially sought to appear as counsel for the Acero Group. codilla:
● FACTS: In the 2001 elections Codilla won as Representative of Leyte’s 4th District over Locsin. A disqualification case was filed against him for allegedly soliciting votes. Without proper notice or a finding that the evidence of guilt was strong, the COMELEC Second Division ordered the suspension of his proclamation and disqualified him, directing the proclamation of Locsin, the second placer. Locsin was proclaimed and took her oath, but Codilla’s motion for reconsideration was granted by the COMELEC en banc, which nullified Locsin’s proclamation and affirmed Codilla’s victory. Locsin refused to vacate, claiming the HRET now had jurisdiction. Codilla filed a petition to compel the House Speaker and Secretary-General to recognize him.
● ISSUE: Was Locsin’s proclamation valid? Did her proclamation and oath-taking remove COMELEC’s jurisdiction (now HRET)? Were the House Speaker and Secretary-General bound to recognize Codilla under the final COMELEC ruling?
● DOCTRINE: A proclamation made without due process is void. Votes for a candidate who has not been disqualified by final judgment cannot be considered stray, and the second placer cannot be proclaimed. A motion for reconsideration suspends the effect of a COMELEC Division’s ruling, so jurisdiction remains with the COMELEC until its decision becomes final. Once the COMELEC’s decision is final, the Speaker and Secretary-General have a ministerial duty to recognize the rightful winner.
● The doctrinal ruling that once a proclamation has been made and a candidate-elect has assumed office, it is [the HRET] that has jurisdiction over an election contest involving members of the House of Representatives, could not have been immediately applicable due to the issue regarding the validity of the very COMELEC pronouncement themselves. This is because the HRET has no jurisdiction to review resolutions or decisions of the COMELEC.
● RULING: The Court ruled that Locsin’s proclamation was invalid because Codilla was denied due process and his disqualification was not yet final. The COMELEC en banc properly retained jurisdiction, as the HRET could not assume authority over a non-final ruling. The Court granted Codilla’s petition and ordered the Speaker to administer his oath and the Secretary-General to enroll his name in the official Roll of Members of the House of Representatives [considered as ministerial duties].
velasco:

Despite this, she was still proclaimed winner. The Supreme Court later upheld the cancellation, declaring her proclamation void. COMELEC then proclaimed Lord Allan Jay Velasco as the rightful winner. However, Speaker Feliciano Belmonte, Jr. and Secretary-General Marilyn Barua-Yap refused to administer Velasco’s oath or record his name in the Roll of Members. Since Reyes’s COC was cancelled before her proclamation, she never became a member of the House. Once Velasco was lawfully proclaimed, the duties of the Speaker and Secretary-General to administer his oath and record his name became purely ministerial.
● The Speaker and Secretary-General of the HoR are legally duty-bound to follow the final and executory Decisions and Resolution of the SC and the COMELEC. The acts of administration of oath and registration in Roll of Members of the rightful candidate are ministerial in character and not a matter of discretion.
● Velasco is declared the winner because Reyes’ COC was declared invalid prior to the elections, thus the votes of Reyes were stray and invalid.

Composition:
daza:
● FACTS: After the 1987 elections, Raul Daza (Liberal Party) was elected as one of the House’s 12 representatives to the Commission on Appointments (CA). In 1988, 24 LP members defected to the newly formed Laban ng Demokratikong Pilipino (LDP), reducing LP’s House membership. The House then reorganized the CA to reflect the new party alignments, replacing Daza with Luis Singson (LDP). Daza challenged his removal, arguing that his CA seat was permanent and that the LDP was not yet a registered or stable party.
● The Court held that the House has the authority to change its representation in the Commission on Appointments to reflect at any time the changes in the political alignments of its membership. However, the changes must be permanent and must involve severance of political loyalties or formal disaffiliation & permanent shifts of allegiance, not merely temporary alliances or factional divisions.
● The Supreme Court dismissed the petition and upheld the reorganization. It ruled that the House validly replaced Daza with Singson because the shift of 24 members from the LP to the LDP was a permanent realignment, requiring the CA’s composition to be adjusted to maintain proportional representation
coseteng:
● Coseteng, the lone member of KAIBA, sought a seat at CA and HRET, claiming that she had 9 endorsements from other members.
● Petition should be dismissed because the revision of the House representation in the Commission on Appointments is based on proportional representation of the political parties therein as provided in Section 18, Article VI of the 1987 Constitution
● The threshold for CoA seats is that to be entitled to 1 seat out of 12 House seats in the CoA, a political party must represent at least 1/12th or 8.4% of the total House membership equating to electing at least 17 representatives.
● KAIBA, with lone member Rep. Coseteng, did not meet this (0.4% > 1%). Endorsement from 9 other Congresspersons did not confer entitlement because they are not members of her party and also endorsed another candidate
drilondevenecia:
● FACTS: Two petitions questioned the composition of the CA for violating proportional representation. In G.R. No. 180055 (1st petition), the LP claimed it was entitled to one House seat in the CA based on its 20-member strength, but its request was delayed or denied. In G.R. No. 183055 (2nd petition), Senator Madrigal alleged that both Senate and House contingents were improperly composed, with certain parties being overrepresented, and asked the Court to order a reorganization.
● ISSUE: Did the composition of the CA violate the constitutional rule on proportional party representation? Can the Supreme Court compel Congress to reorganize the CA?
● DOCTRINE: The Court held that only the Senate and the House have the constitutional power to elect their CA members. Under the doctrine of primary jurisdiction, complaints about CA representation must first be raised before the respective chamber. The Supreme Court may only intervene if a House clearly refuses to fulfill its constitutional duty. Petitioners must also show locus standi by proving a direct and personal injury.
● RULING: The first petition was dismissed as moot since the Liberal Party later received a CA seat. The second petition was dismissed for lack of standing and prematurity because Senator Madrigal failed to show her party suffered direct injury and had not first raised her claims before the Senate.
guingonagonzales:
● FACTS: After the 1992 elections, the Senate was divided among four groups: Party # of Senators Proportional Seats Laban ng Demokratikong 15 7.5 Pilipino (LDP) National People’s Coalition 5 2.5 (NPC) LAKAS-NUCD 3 1.5 LD-PDP-LABAN 1 (Sen. Tañada) 0.5
● Despite being entitled to only 7.5 seats, the LDP nominated eight members, including Senator Alberto Romulo, and also gave Senator Wigberto Tañada (LP-PDP-LABAN) a full seat. Senator Guingona, representing LAKAS-NUCD, objected and filed a petition, arguing this violated the constitutional rule of proportional representation by giving the majority party more than its fair share.
● ISSUE: Did the election of Senators Romulo and Tañada to the Commission on Appointments comply with the constitutional rule of proportional representation?
● DOCTRINE: No. The Constitution (Article VI, Section 18) requires strict proportional representation of political parties in the CA. This rule is mandatory and cannot be altered by majority vote or compromise. The Court held that even fractional entitlements must be respected; adding or rounding up seats in favor of one party distorts proportionality. It also clarified that a party must have at least two senators per CA seat, so a party with only one senator cannot constitutionally hold a CA seat. The legality of CA membership is a justiciable, not political, issue.
● In order to obtain a seat in the Commission, (1) a party must have at least 2 senators, and (2) if there are more than 2 parties, then a party with a lone senator could not claim a seat.
● The Constitution does not require the presence of 12 Senator-members in the CA, ruling that the CA could function with only 4 members from each House.
● RULING: The Supreme Court declared the election of Senators Romulo and Tañada null and void for violating proportional representation. It ruled that the LDP majority acted with grave abuse of discretion by giving itself and the LP-PDP-LABAN more than their rightful share. The Court issued a writ of prohibition, preventing Romulo and Tanada from serving in the CA, and ordering the Senate President to stop recognizing them. Powers of Congress
sema:
● The 1987 Constitution apportioned Maguindanao into 2 districts, the first including Cotabato City and 8 municipalities. Maguindanao joined ARMM but Cotabato City did not. In 2006, the ARMM Regional Assembly passed MMA Act 201 creating Shariff Kabunsuan Province from those 8 municipalities. COMELEC issued Reso. 7902 renaming the first district as “Shariff Kabunsuan and Cotabato City”.
● Petitioner Sema, a candidate for representative, assailed this, arguing that only Congress can create legislative districts and COMELEC usurped legislative power
● The Court ruled that Sec. 19, Article VI of RA 9054 is unconstitutional for granting the ARMM the authority to create provinces and cities. Since creating a province entails creating a legislative district, the power belongs solely to Congress and cannot be delegated.
○ But COMELEC Reso 7902 was valid .
● Only Congress has the plenary power to create legislative districts under Art. VI, Sec. 5 of the Constitution. The creation of a province or city automatically entails the creation of a district; a national legislative act cannot be delegated to regional assemblies.
○ By the principle of expressio unius est exclusio alterius, the Constitution is silent on giving autonomous regions this authority. Therefore, they do not have such power.
torralba:
● Petitioners are assailing the constitutionality of BP 56 which created the Municipality of Sibagat. Under Sec. 3, Art. XI of the 1973 Consti, a Local Government Code must first be enacted to determine the criteria for the creation, division, merger, abolition, or substantial alteration of the boundary of any province, city, municipality, or barrio
● It is a long-recognized principle that the power to create a municipal corporation is essentially legislative in nature. In the absence of any constitutional limitations, a legislative body may create any corporation it deems essential for the more efficient administration of government. The absence of an LGC at the time of BP 56 did not curtail nor was it intended to cripple legislative competence to create municipal corporations
● What the Constitutional provision means is that once said Code is enacted, the creation, modification or dissolution of local government units should conform with the criteria thus laid down. In the interregnum, before the enactment of such Code, the legislative power remains plenary except that the creation of the new local government unit should be approved by the people concerned in a plebiscite called for the purpose.
● The creation of the Municipality of Sibagat satisfied all mandatory requisites: a plebiscite was conducted and approved by the voters of the unit/units affected, and the appointed municipal officers took their oaths and performed their duties; thus creating a de jure entity.
abakada:
● RA 9335 was enacted to optimize revenue generation of the BIR and BOC. Art. 12 of RA 9335 prescribes a Joint Congressional Oversight Committee (JCOC), composed of members of Congress, to approve the IRR formulated by the agencies concerned. Petitioners assail this as an alleged encroachment on the executive function of “implementing and enforcing the law” by the Congress
● Categories of congressional oversight functions a. Scrutiny - a lesser intensity and continuity of attention to administrative operations. Congress may ask for reports/info from other branches b. Congressional investigation - a more intense digging of facts c. Legislative supervision - third and most encompassing form, connoting a continuing and informed awareness on the part of a congressional committee regarding executive operations; allows Congress to scrutinize the exercise of delegated law-making authority. Legislative veto - Congress retains a “right” to approve or disapprove any regulation before it takes effect
● Any post-enactment congressional measure should be limited to scrutiny and investigation. Any action or step beyond that will undermine the separation of powers, such as legislative vetoes.
● A provision that requires Congress or its members to approve the implementing rules of a law after it has already taken effect shall be unconstitutional, as it allows Congress or its members to overturn any directive or ruling made by the members of the executive branch charged with the implementation of the law.
● RULING: The Court partially granted the petition: Section 12 of R.A. 9335 was struck down as unconstitutional for granting Congress the power to approve the IRR, which encroaches on executive functions and bypasses constitutional lawmaking procedures. The rest of the law was upheld due to its separability clause, making the reward and sanction system for BIR and BOC personnel valid.
lidasan:
● RA 4790, entitled “An Act creating the Municipality of Dianaton in the Province of Lanao del Sur”, is being assailed by Bara Lidasan as unconstitutional because not all the barrios listed in RA 4790 belongs to the municipality of Butig and Balabagan in the province of Lanao del Sur as the statute claims. 12 of the Barrios are in Cotabato.
● Bills must not embrace more than one subject expressed in the title. This constitutional provision contains dual limitations upon legislative power: (1) Congress is to refrain from conglomeration, under one statute, of heterogeneous subjects; (2) the title to the bills is to be couched in a language sufficient to notify the legislators and the public and those concerned of the import of the single subject thereof.
● A title is defective if it is misleading, restrictive, or fails to reflect essential matters embraced in the law. Validity also depends on inseparability: if the unconstitutional parts are integral to the whole, the entire law is void.
● RULING: The Court declared R.A. 4790 unconstitutional in its entirety. The law’s title referred only to Lanao del Sur, but its body also detached barrios from Cotabato, misleading legislators and residents about the law’s true scope. Since the creation of Dianaton was premised on all 21 barrios, removing the 12 Cotabato barrios would alter viability and legislative intent, making the valid and invalid parts inseparable. Thus, the whole Act was struck down and COMELEC was prohibited from implementing it.
● The title must serve the purpose of the constitutional demand that it informs the legislators (persons interested in the subject of the bill) and the public of the nature, scope and consequences of the proposed law and its operation to lead them to inquire into the body of the bill and prevent surprise or fraud upon the legislators.
cruzparas:
● Petitioners, operators of nightclubs and cabarets in Bocaue, Bulacan, challenged Municipal Ordinance No. 84 - “Prohibition and Closure Ordinance”, which prohibited the operation of nightclubs, cabaret, and dance halls, and revoked existing licenses and permits.
● The title of RA 938 only contained ‘Regulate’ and Sec 1 granted the power to only regulate, not prohibit. Later, when the law was amended, the body gave power to municipalities to ‘Prohibit or Regulate’. However, the title of the amended law stayed the same.
● Article VI, Section 26(1) 1987 Constitution: "Every bill shall embrace only one subject which shall be expressed in the title thereof." , therefore, with two possible interpretations, one that makes it constitutional shall be followed. In this case, the municipal ordinance in question is deemed null.
● The Local Government Code expressly grants municipalities - sangguniang bayan - authority to regulate establishments and forms of entertainment, reinforcing the limitation already found in RA No. 938.
●
RULING: The Court struck down Ordinance No. 84 as null and unconstitutional, holding that the municipality had no authority to prohibit the operation of nightclubs and cabarets since the enabling law’s title limited their power to regulation. The prohibition was unreasonable and overbroad, as the municipality could have achieved its goal of protecting public morals through regulatory measures rather than an outright ban. The petition was granted, reversing the lower court’s ruling.
giron:
● FACTS: Henry Giron assailed the constitutionality of Sections 12 and 14 of the Fair Election Act (R.A. 9006), claiming they violated the “one subject–one title” rule under Article VI, Section 26(1) of the 1987 Constitution. He argued that provisions on substitution of candidates and repeal of Section 67 of the Omnibus Election Code were unrelated to the law’s supposed subject of lifting the political ad ban.
● ISSUE: Whether the inclusion of Sections 12 and 14 in the Fair Election Act violates the constitutional requirement that every bill must embrace only one subject expressed in its title.
● DOCTRINE: The constitutional rule on titles of bills prevents surprise or fraud and ensures legislators and the public are informed of a bill’s scope. It does not require the title to be a complete index of its contents. An act having a single general subject may contain any number or diversity of provisions, as long as they are not inconsistent with or foreign to the general subject, and may be considered in furtherance of the subject by providing for the method and means of it.
● RULING: The Court dismissed the petition, holding that Sections 12 and 14 of R.A. 9006 do not violate the one subject–one title rule. The title and objectives of the Fair Election Act were broad enough to cover substitution of candidates and repeal of automatic resignation provisions. Requiring the law’s title to list every detail would cripple legislation, and records showed Congress deliberately framed the title to encompass election reforms beyond the ad ban. Q: Can the longer title of a bill cure a defect in its shorter title? (e.g. Bayanihan to Heal as One) A: No, because the purpose of the constitutional directive on the titles of bills is to apprise the legislators of the purposes, the nature and scope of its provisions. The bill is more often referred to by the legislators and the general public by its shorter name, and its nature must already be clear from this title alone. (In the first reading of bills, titles are heavily depended on.)

philconsaenriquez:
● FACTS: House Bill No. 10900, or the General Appropriations Bill of 1994, was passed by Congress and signed into law as RA 7663. The President, however, vetoed several provisions and imposed conditions on others, including those relating to the Countrywide Development Fund (pork barrel), fund realignments, and appropriations for debt service, SUCs, AFP, DPWH, and constitutional bodies. Petitioners questioned the constitutionality of the CDF, realignment powers, prioritization of debt service over education, and the validity of presidential vetoes and conditions.
DOCTRINES
● Power of Appropriation – Congress has the power to appropriate and specify the project or activity to be funded under the appropriation law which can be as detailed or broad as it wants to be. Under the CDF, legislators can propose and identify projects to be implemented by the President as it will be subject to the approval of the latter. → merely recommendatory
● Realignment of Savings – Only authorized officials (President, SP, Speaker, CJ, heads of constitutional commissions) may realign savings; members of Congress may only recommend realignment subject to approval.
● Priority of Education – Constitution requires education to be given highest priority, but Congress retains discretion to allocate funds considering national interests (e.g., debt service).
● Item Veto Power – The Constitution is explicit that what Congress can include in a GAB must relate specifically to some particular appropriation therein and be limited in its operation to the appropriation it relates. When the legislature inserts inappropriate provisions in a general appropriation bill, such provisions must be treated as 'items' for purposes of the Governor's item veto power over general appropriation bills.
● “Inappropriate provisions” - those unrelated to appropriations, or which amend substantive law or where it is better suited to be enacted in a separate legislation → must be vetoed
RULING: Petitions were generally dismissed, upholding the constitutionality of the CDF (recommendatory only) and validity of most presidential vetoes/conditions. However, the Court struck down vetoes that invalidly separated “appropriate provisions” inseparable from the appropriated items—such as (1) parts of the debt service item, (2) the 70/30 DPWH road maintenance ratio, and (3) AFP medicine purchases. Thus, most vetoes and conditions were sustained, but select vetoes were declared unconstitutional.
lamp:
● LAMP filed a petition to declare PDAF unconstitutional arguing that DBM illegally made and directly released budgetary allocations to individual legislators.
● Presumption of Constitutionality – Appropriation laws are presumed valid; to strike them down requires clear, convincing proof of constitutional breach.
● Power of Appropriation vs. Execution – Congress has the “power of the purse” to appropriate, but budget execution belongs to the Executive; legislators may only recommend projects.
● Inadequacy of Speculation – Media reports, conjectures, or general allegations of misuse cannot overturn appropriation statutes without factual and documentary evidence.
● RULING: The Court dismissed the petition, holding that the 2004 PDAF was valid and constitutional. Petitioners failed to prove that funds were released directly to legislators or that they exercised control over spending. Congress’ role was limited to recommending projects, while implementation and disbursement were handled by the Executive. In the absence of clear evidence of constitutional violation, the presumption of validity of appropriation laws stood, and the separation of powers remained intact
belgica2013:
● Petitioners question the constitutionality of the PDAF in the 2013 GAA and the Presidential Pork Barrel (Malampaya Funds and the Presidential Social Fund)
● The Pork Barrel System allowed legislators to identify projects and programs to be financed by the government after the enactment. This gave legislators a postenactment role that amounted to legislative supervision and transcended scrutiny and investigation.
○ Overturned the rulings in PHILCONSA v. Enriquez and LAMP v. Secretary of Budget which upheld the validity of forms of pork barrel.
○ Legislative power is limited to law-making, save for the oversight powers of scrutiny and investigation.
● The Pork Barrel system was unconstitutional for violating the rule on the separation of powers. Also violates non-delegability of legislative power since legislative power is exercised by the bicameral body (both Houses). PDAF confers authority to individual legislators to appropriate funds by allowing them to identify and choose projects. It allowed legislators to intervene and/or assume duties that properly belong to the sphere of budget execution → which belongs to the Executive. This is no longer “recommendatory”, because without the individual legislator’s participation, the PDAF cannot be utilized.
● To ensure that the President may be able to exercise his power of item veto, an item of appropriation must be an item characterized by singular correspondence — meaning an allocation of a specified singular amount for a specified singular purpose, otherwise known as a "line-item."
● PDAF also violates the principle of checks and balances since it deprives the President the power to veto any particular item in an appropriations bill since the PDAF is a lump-sum appropriation and that the projects are identified after the enactment of the budget, this is an intermediate appropriation (a budget within a budget). Congress cannot check on its members.
● Congressional Pork Barrel goes against the principles of local autonomy by allowing district representatives, who are national officers, to substitute their judgements in utilising funds for local developments
● On the President’s lump sum funds: While discretionary funds in themselves are not unconstitutional, disbursement of such funds must meet the requirements for a valid delegation of legislative power.
● The Court upheld the validity of the Presidential Social Fund, and the Malampaya Fund, which were funds disbursed under the discretion of the President but invalidated provisions of the laws establishing these funds which gave the President wide latitude in disbursing these funds without legislative guidelines.
belgica2019:
● FACTS: After the 2013 Belgica ruling struck down the PDAF as unconstitutional, Belgica challenged the validity of several lump-sum appropriations in the 2014 GAA—namely the Unprogrammed Fund, Contingent Fund, E-Government Fund, and Local Government Support Fund—arguing that they violated the constitutional requirement that appropriations must state a specific purpose and not leave undue discretion to the Executive.
● DOCTRINE: Appropriation laws must embody the rule of singular correspondence—each “item” means a specific sum for a specific purpose. Lump-sum funds are not per se unconstitutional; they are valid if they serve a discernible single purpose, contain sufficient standards to guide execution, and do not negate the President’s veto power. Only lump-sums that fund multiple unrelated purposes with vague standards, such as the PDAF, are unconstitutional.
● Prohibited Lump-sum Appropriations - do not indicate a specific appropriation or purpose for the money, hence there is no proper line item the president may veto; pres can only veto it as a whole or not at all – generally unconstitutional
● Allowed Lump-sum Appropriations - a lump-sum amount may still be considered as a valid item subject to the President's item veto power for as long as:
○ the lump-sum amount is meant as a funding source for multiple programs, projects, or activities that may all be clearly classified as falling under one singular appropriation purpose.
○ This singular purpose may be as general or specific as the legislative department deems it to be, provided that such generality or specificity does not negate the President's proper exercise of his item veto power. (not multiple unrelated purposes nor vague and amorphous)
● RULING: The Court upheld the constitutionality of the Unprogrammed Fund, Contingent Fund, E-Government Fund, and Local Government Support Fund in the 2014 GAA, ruling that each had a clear singular purpose and sufficient legislative standards. Unlike the PDAF, these funds did not involve post-enactment discretion by legislators nor negate the line-item veto. The petition was dismissed for lack of merit.

● FACTS: The Disbursement Acceleration Program (DAP) was created in 2011 as an executive fiscal strategy to accelerate spending by pooling unobligated allotments, unreleased appropriations, and unprogrammed funds. Petitioners challenged its constitutionality, arguing that it violated the Constitution’s rules on appropriations, savings, and augmentation of funds, which are powers reserved to Congress.
● 3 Requisites of Section 25 (5), Article VI:
1. There is a law authorizing the President to transfer funds within his office (i.e. the GAA)
2. That there are savings or any programmed appropriation in the GAA free from any obligation (when a project is completed or discontinued, efficiency savings or balances from unfilled plantilla at the end of the year)
3. Purpose of the transfer is to augment an item in the GAA for their respective offices
● While the President has discretion in implementing the budget, this does not translate to an unfettered discretion that allowed the President to substitute his own will for that of Congress. Since DAP also transferred funds to the COA and HoR, which are not under the President’s offices, it is considered a cross-border transaction and is prohibited under Sec. 25(5), Art. VI.
● Further, what the Executive determined as savings were contrary to what was prescribed in the GAA, which stated that savings only exist when funds allocated for a specific purpose have been already satisfied or the need for such funds have ceased to exist. Also, it was shown in the evidence that savings pooled under DAP were allocated to items not covered by any appropriation in the GAA.
● RULING: The Court declared unconstitutional the following DAP practices: (1) declaring savings from withdrawn unobligated allotments before the end of the fiscal year, (2) cross-border transfers of executive savings to other branches or constitutional bodies, (3) funding projects not covered by the GAA, and (4) use of unprogrammed funds without certification of excess revenues. However, the DAP itself as a strategy was not invalid per se. Completed projects funded under DAP are recognized under the doctrine of operative fact, but officials responsible may still be held liable.

● FACTS: Petitioners questioned the legality of the LTO’s ₱3.85-billion Motor Vehicle License Plate Standardization Program (MVPSP), funded under the 2014 GAA. They alleged irregular use of funds and the lack of a valid Multi-Year Obligational Authority. The COA later disallowed ₱477.9 million in advance payments to the contractor JKG-Power Plates for being illegal. (not raised)
● ISSUE: (1) W/N using the 2014 GAA appropriation to fund the MVPSP was an unconstitutional transfer of funds, (2) W/N the Major Final Output appropriation was an unconstitutional lump-sum
● DOCTRINE: To be valid, an appropriation must indicate a specific amount and a specific purpose. A specific purpose encompasses sub-categories that are naturally included in such.
● RULING:
● (1) No. Under the Major Final Output (MFO) Item “Motor Vehicle Registration and Driver’s Licensing Regulatory Services,” this naturally includes plate-making inasmuch as plate-making is an integral component of the registration process.
● (2) No. The Court held that under the 2014 GAA’s Performance-Informed Budgeting system, “Major Final Outputs” (MFOs) are merely broad categories, not specific appropriations. A valid budget “item” must have a definite purpose and amount that can be subject to presidential veto. pichay:
● President Aquino abolished the Presidential Anti-Graft Commission (PAGC) and transferred its functions to the newly created Investigative and Adjudicatory Division (IAD) of the Office of the Deputy Executive Secretary for Legal Affairs (ODESLA). A case against Pichay was filed before the ODESLA. Pichay is questioning the creation of the IAD and the appropriation of funds by the president in the EO 13.
● The president is given discretion to augment items in the appropriations act for offices under his authority using savings from appropriations made for other items under his office. This authority, however, is limited. The President has continuing authority to reorganize his office under the Administrative Code.
● RULING: EO 13 is constitutional. SC held that the President validly reorganized the Office of the President by abolishing the PAGC and transferring its functions to ODESLA under Section 31 of the Administrative Code, which authorizes such reorganization for efficiency. The IAD-ODESLA was not a new office with quasi-judicial powers but merely a fact-finding and recommendatory body, consistent with the President’s power of control and duty to ensure laws are faithfully executed. No usurpation of legislative or appropriation powers occurred, since the IAD was funded within the President’s existing budget under the GAA and constitutional authority to realign savings. There was no encroachment upon the Ombudsman’s jurisdiction, as administrative investigations may be concurrently conducted by the President. Lastly, due process and equal protection were not violated: Pichay was given the chance to respond, and the classification of presidential appointees for investigation was reasonable given the President’s disciplinary authority over them.
nazareth:
● FACTS: DOST Region IX personnel in Zamboanga City received Magna Carta benefits under R.A. 8439 from 1998 to 2001, despite the absence of a specific appropriation in the GAA. The regional office used its savings to fund these payments, which later led the COA to issue Notices of Disallowance after post-audit. In 2000, DOST Secretary Filemon Uriarte sought and obtained presidential approval from Executive Secretary Ronaldo Zamora to continue using savings for these benefits. COA lifted the disallowances for 1998 to 2000, as they were covered by the presidential approval, but upheld the 2001 disallowance, ruling that the approval did not extend to that year. Brenda Nazareth, the DOST Regional Director, then alleged that COA gravely abused its discretion in maintaining the 2001 disallowance.
● DOCTRINE: No money shall be paid out of the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law. Violation warrants disallowance. A government agency cannot claim benefits if these benefits are not specifically appropriated for by law.
● RULING: SC upheld COA’s disallowance of the 2001 payments, finding no grave abuse of discretion. It held that under Article VI, Section 29(1), no public funds may be disbursed without an appropriation made by law, and R.A. 8439 expressly requires Magna Carta benefits to be funded through the GAA. The President’s power to augment appropriations under Article VI, Section 25(5) applies only when there are actual savings and an existing item to be augmented. Since the April 12, 2000 Memorandum authorizing the use of DOST savings covered only 1998–2000, and no authority or appropriation existed for 2001, the payments were unconstitutional and illegal.
madera:
● FACTS: The Municipality of Mondragon, Northern Samar, issued several ordinances and resolutions granting allowances such as Economic Crisis Assistance, Monetary Augmentation, Agricultural Crisis Assistance, and Mitigation Allowance to local and national employees, totaling ₱7.7 million. The COA issued 11 Notices of Disallowance in February 2014, citing violations of the Salary Standardization Law (R.A. 6758), DBM circulars, and CSC rules. The approving officers—including the mayor, accountant, treasurer, and budget officer—were held liable, while recipients were excused due to good faith. After the COA Regional Director and COA Proper upheld the disallowances, the approving officers filed for certiorari before the Supreme Court.
● DOCTRINE: Allowances and benefits not expressly exempted under Section 12 of R.A. 6758 are deemed integrated into standardized salaries, and their grant without legal basis is void even if done in good faith or by long practice.
● RULING: The Supreme Court affirmed the validity of the disallowances. It held that under Section 12 of R.A. 6758, all allowances are integrated into standardized salaries except for a few expressly exempted ones—none of which included the benefits granted by the municipality. The Sangguniang Bayan’s authority under the Local Government Code cannot override the Salary Standardization Law, and the two statutes must be harmonized.
● The Court further ruled that benefits given by mere practice do not create vested rights, especially when they lack a lawful basis or connection to the employees’ official functions.
● The Court holds that petitioners, as approving and certifying officers, need not refund the disallowed amounts because they acted in good faith. Rules on Returns of Notice of Disallowances
● If a Notice of Disallowance is set aside by the Court, no return shall be required from any of the persons held liable therein.
● If a Notice of Disallowance is upheld, the rules on return are as follows:
■ Approving and certifying officers who acted in good faith, are not civilly liable to return
■ Approving and certifying officers who are clearly shown to have acted in bad faith, malice, or gross negligence are solidarily liable to return only the net disallowed amount (total disallowed amount minus amount excused to be returned by the payees)
■ Recipients — whether approving or certifying officers or mere passive recipients — are liable to return the disallowed amounts respectively received by them, unless they are able to show that the amounts they received were genuinely given in consideration of services rendered.
■ The Court may likewise excuse the return of recipients based on undue prejudice, social justice considerations, and other bona fide exceptions as it may determine on a case to case basis. b. Tax laws Sec. 28, Art. VI.
tolentinofinance:
● FACTS: Multiple petitions were filed challenging the constitutionality of R.A. 7716, the Expanded VAT Law, which sought to widen the VAT base and improve tax collection. Petitioners claimed the law was invalid for procedural defects—arguing it did not properly originate from the House, violated the three-reading rule, and exceeded the Conference Committee’s powers. They also raised substantive issues, alleging violations of press and religious freedom, due process, equal protection, and the constitutional ban on regressive taxes.
● Tax Bills shall originate exclusively in the House of Representatives: it is not the law, but the revenue bill, which is required by the Constitution to “originate exclusively” in the House of Representatives.
● A bill originating in the House may undergo such extensive changes in the Senate that the result may be a rewriting of the whole. As a result of the Senate action, a distinct bill may be produced.
● To insist that it must substantially be the same as the House bill would:
○ deny the Senate's power to “concur with amendments” and to “propose amendments.”
○ violate the co-equality of legislative power of the two houses of Congress
○ make the House superior to the Senate.
● What the Constitution simply means is that the initiative for filing revenue, tariff, or tax bills, bills authorizing an increase of the public debt, private bills and bills of local application must come from the House of Representatives on the theory that, elected as they are from the districts, the members of the House can be expected to be more sensitive to the local needs and problems. On the other hand, senators, who are elected at large, are expected to approach the same problems from the national perspective. Both views are thereby made to bear on the enactment of such laws.
● The Constitution does not prohibit the filing in the Senate of a substitute bill in anticipation of its receipt of the bill from the House, so long as action by the Senate as a body is withheld pending receipt of the House bill.
● The presidential certification also dispensed with the requirement not only of printing but also that of reading the bill on separate days.
● The Court held that it is within the power of a conference committee to include in its report an entirely new provision that is not found either in the House Bill or in the Senate Bill, and they are not constrained to only consider conflicting provisions.
● The provision on a progressive system of taxation is not self-executory. It is an incentive to legislate, and does not constitute an enforceable right.
lungcenter:
● FACTS: The Lung Center of the Philippines, a non-stock, non-profit entity created by P.D. No. 1823 in 1981, owns a 121,463 sq. m. lot in Quezon City where its hospital operates. It provides services to both paying and non-paying patients and receives annual government subsidies. Portions of its property are leased commercially: ground floor spaces for a canteen and stores, hospital spaces to private medical practitioners, and a large land area to Elliptical Orchids and Garden Center. Petitioner filed a Claim for Exemption from real property taxes on the claim that it is a charitable institution
● City Assessor denied → Local Board of Assessment Appeals of QC dismissed → Central Board of Assessment Appeals of QC affirmed QC-LBAA’s decision → CA affirmed CBAA’s decision (petitioner was not a charitable institution and that its real properties were not actually, directly and exclusively used for charitable purposes; hence, it was not entitled to real property tax exemption under the constitution and the law)
● Definition of Charitable Organization or Institution: charity may be fully defined as a gift for the benefit of an indefinite number of persons; It may be applied to almost anything that tends to promote the well-doing and well-being of a social man. It embraces the improvement and promotion of the happiness of man. The word “charitable” is not restricted to relief of the poor or sick. The test whether an enterprise is charitable or not is whether it exists to carry out a purpose reorganized in law as a charitable or whether it is maintained for gain, profit, or private advantage.
● For charitable institutions, the exemption from property tax is for the land, building and improvements, actually, directly, and exclusively used for charitable purposes (Section 28 (3), Article VI)
○ If real property is used for one or more commercial purposes, it is not exclusively used for the exempted purposes but is subject to taxation. Solely is synonymous with exclusively.
○ Actual, direct, and exclusive use of the property for charitable purposes - the direct and immediate and actual application of the property itself to the purposes for which the charitable institution is organized. It is not the use of the income from the real property that is determinative of whether the property is used for tax-exempt purposes
● RULING: The petitioner failed to discharge its burden to prove that the entirety of its real property is actually, directly and exclusively used for charitable purposes
● Other portions of the hospital are leased to private individuals for their clinics and a canteen; Portion of land is being leased for a business enterprise “Elliptical Orchids and Garden Center” - these parts are not exempt from RP taxes
● Portions of land occupied by the hospital and portions of the hospital used for its patients, whether for paying or non-paying, are exempt from RP taxes
garciaexecsec:
● FACTS: President Ramos issued EO No. 438, imposing an additional 5% ad valorem duty on all imports, including crude oil and oil products. EO No. 443 increased this additional duty to 9% ad valorem. The Department of Finance requested the Tariff Commission to begin procedures for imposing a specific levy on crude oil and petroleum products, prompting the Commission to hold a public hearing under Section 401 of the Tariff and Customs Code. EO No. 475 reduced the additional duty on all imports back to 5%, except for crude oil and oil products, which remained at 9%. Then, EO No. 478 imposed a special duty of ₱0.95 per liter on imported crude oil and ₱1.00 per liter on imported oil products, in addition to existing duties. Congressman Garcia filed a petition questioning the validity of EOs 475 and 478.
● DOCTRINE: The enactment of appropriation, revenue and tariff bills, like all other bills, is within the province of the Legislative rather than the Executive Department. But under Sec 28(2), Art 6, there is explicit constitutional permission for Congress to authorize the President “subject to such limitations and restrictions as [Congress] may impose” to fix “within specific limits” “tariff rates ... and other duties or imposts...”
● RULING: The Court upheld the validity of 2 executive orders subjecting crude oil and other oil products to special duties pursuant to the power delegated to the President under the Tariff and Customs Code. Section 401 grants broad authority to adjust tariffs for general welfare. The President’s authority must be exercised in "the interest of national economy, general welfare and/or national security.", as provided by the Tariff and Customs Code. The concept of the “protection of local industries” as the only permissible objective for the exercise of that delegated authority is stiflingly narrow → Court cannot build it into the Constitution and Customs Law.
● Accordingly, we believe and so hold that Executive Orders Nos. 475 and 478 which may be conceded to be substantially moved by the desire to generate additional public revenues, are not, for that reason alone, either constitutionally flawed, or legally infirm under Section 401 of the Tariff and Customs Code.
johnhay:
● FACTS: R.A. No. 7227, the Bases Conversion and Development Act of 1992, aimed to convert former U.S. military bases, including Camp John Hay in Baguio City, into productive civilian uses and created the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) to manage these areas. The law authorized the President, with the LGU, to establish Special Economic Zones (SEZs) in these base areas. FVR issued Proclamation No. 420 on July 5, 1994, officially creating the JHSEZ and granting it the same incentives as the Subic SEZ, including tax and duty-free importation and exemption from local and national taxes. Residents and city councilors of Baguio City filed a petition challenging the constitutionality of Proclamation No. 420
● The Supreme Court, however, said that the tax exemption in RA 7227 is clearly intended for the Subic SEZ only. There is no express extension of the aforesaid benefits to other SEZs still to be created at the time via presidential proclamation
● Proclamation No. 420, insofar as it grants JHSEZ with the benefits of Subic SEZ and more incentives, cannot be sustained. It was an unwarranted delegation.
● Tax exemptions may be granted by Congress: The legislature has the full power to exempt any person or corporation from taxation. Other than Congress, the Constitution may itself provide for specific tax exemptions, or local governments may pass ordinances on exemption only from local taxes.
● The challenged grant of tax exemption would circumvent the Constitution's imposition that a law granting any tax exemption must have the concurrence of a majority of all the members of Congress.
● The other privileges given to John Hay SEZ are also, by tradition and usage, what Congress legislates on
● Tax exemptions cannot be implied, it must be categorically and unmistakably expressed - it must be expressly granted in a statute stated in a language too clear to be mistaken.
● The President cannot, by proclamation, extend tax exemptions absent legislation by Congress.
● This Court then declares that the grant by Proclamation No. 420 of tax exemption and other privileges to the John Hay SEZ is void for being violative of the Constitution.
